blocks.body:
The Riemann hypothesis says that every nontrivial zero of $\zeta(s)$ has real part exactly $\tfrac12$. Nobody can prove it, but for most applications to primes the full statement is not needed. What does the damage is a zero $\rho=\beta+i\gamma$ with $\beta$ close to $1$: through the [[explicit-formula|explicit formula]] it puts a term of size $x^{\beta}$ into $\psi(x)$. A zero-density estimate says that such zeros, if they exist at all, are rare, and the further right you go the rarer they must be.

This lesson defines the counting function $N(\sigma,T)$, explains what shape of bound one can hope for, proves a first density theorem from a mean-value estimate, and shows how density bounds give primes in short intervals.

blocks.title: The zero-counting function N(σ, T)
blocks.body:
For $\tfrac12\le\sigma\le 1$ and $T\ge 2$ put
$$N(\sigma,T)=\#\{\rho=\beta+i\gamma:\ \zeta(\rho)=0,\ \beta\ge\sigma,\ 0<\gamma\le T\},$$
counting zeros with multiplicity. A density estimate is a bound of the form
$$N(\sigma,T)\ll T^{A(1-\sigma)}(\log T)^B\qquad\text{uniformly for } \tfrac12\le\sigma\le1,$$
or the slightly weaker $N(\sigma,T)\ll_\varepsilon T^{A(1-\sigma)+\varepsilon}$.

In words: $N(\sigma,T)$ counts the zeros in the box to the right of the vertical line $\mathrm{Re}\,s=\sigma$ up to height $T$, and the Riemann hypothesis is exactly the statement that $N(\sigma,T)=0$ for every $\sigma>\tfrac12$.

blocks.title: What shape of bound to expect
blocks.body:
Look first at the two ends of the range.

At $\sigma=\tfrac12$: by the Riemann–von Mangoldt formula ([[nontrivial-zeros]]) the total number of zeros with $0<\gamma\le T$ is $N(T)=\frac{T}{2\pi}\log\frac{T}{2\pi}-\frac{T}{2\pi}+O(\log T)$. The map $\rho\mapsto 1-\bar\rho$ sends nontrivial zeros to nontrivial zeros, keeps the ordinate $\gamma$ and swaps $\beta$ with $1-\beta$. So at least half of all zeros have $\beta\ge\tfrac12$, and $N(\tfrac12,T)\ge \tfrac12N(T)\gg T\log T$.

At $\sigma=1$: there are no zeros on the line $\mathrm{Re}\,s=1$, so $N(1,T)=0$. The [[zero-free-region|zero-free region]] gives more: $N(\sigma,T)=0$ once $\sigma\ge 1-c/\log T$.

A bound $T^{A(1-\sigma)}$ interpolates between these: the exponent falls linearly from $A/2$ at $\sigma=\tfrac12$ to $0$ at $\sigma=1$. Since the left side is at least of size $T\log T$ at $\sigma=\tfrac12$, no such bound can hold with $A<2$. The density hypothesis is the conjecture that $A=2$ is admissible:
$$N(\sigma,T)\ll_\varepsilon T^{2(1-\sigma)+\varepsilon}.$$
It follows from the Riemann hypothesis trivially and from the [[lindelof|Lindelöf hypothesis]] by a theorem of Ingham.

Uniformity in $\sigma$ matters because applications integrate over $\sigma$: a zero with real part $\beta$ costs $x^{\beta-1}$ relative to the main term, and the bound must beat that cost for every $\beta$ at once.

blocks.title: The main density theorems
blocks.body:
1. Bohr and Landau (1914): for each fixed $\sigma>\tfrac12$, $N(\sigma,T)=O_\sigma(T)$.
2. Carlson (1920): $N(\sigma,T)\ll_\varepsilon T^{4\sigma(1-\sigma)+\varepsilon}$.
3. Ingham (1940): $N(\sigma,T)\ll T^{3(1-\sigma)/(2-\sigma)}(\log T)^5$. Since $3/(2-\sigma)\le 3$, this gives $A=3$.
4. Huxley (1972): $N(\sigma,T)\ll T^{3(1-\sigma)/(3\sigma-1)}(\log T)^B$ for $\tfrac34\le\sigma\le1$. Combined with Ingham's bound for $\sigma\le\tfrac34$ (the two exponents agree at $\sigma=\tfrac34$, where both equal $\tfrac{12}{5}(1-\sigma)$), this gives $A=\tfrac{12}{5}$.
5. Guth and Maynard (2024): $N(\sigma,T)\ll_\varepsilon T^{15(1-\sigma)/(3+5\sigma)+\varepsilon}$, which beats the older bounds for $\tfrac{7}{10}<\sigma<\tfrac{8}{10}$. Combined with Ingham and Huxley this gives $A=\tfrac{30}{13}$ (with an $\varepsilon$).

The density hypothesis $A=2$ remains open; it is known only for $\sigma$ sufficiently close to $1$ (Huxley's bound alone gives it for $\sigma\ge\tfrac56$, where $3/(3\sigma-1)\le2$).

blocks.title: Zeros are detected by mean values
blocks.body:
Why should averages of $|\zeta|$ say anything about zeros? Jensen's formula from complex analysis already says that the number of zeros of a holomorphic function in a disc is controlled by the average of $\log|f|$ on a larger circle. For rectangles there is a version adapted to counting zeros by their real parts.

Littlewood's lemma. Let $f$ be holomorphic on an open set containing the rectangle $R=\{\sigma_0\le\mathrm{Re}\,s\le\sigma_1,\ t_0\le\mathrm{Im}\,s\le T\}$, with no zeros on the boundary of $R$. For $\sigma_0\le u\le\sigma_1$ let $\nu(u)$ be the number of zeros of $f$ in $R$ with real part greater than $u$. Then
$$2\pi\int_{\sigma_0}^{\sigma_1}\nu(u)\,du=\int_{t_0}^{T}\log|f(\sigma_0+it)|\,dt-\int_{t_0}^{T}\log|f(\sigma_1+it)|\,dt+\int_{\sigma_0}^{\sigma_1}\arg f(u+iT)\,du-\int_{\sigma_0}^{\sigma_1}\arg f(u+it_0)\,du,$$
where $\arg f$ on the horizontal sides is defined by continuous variation starting from the right-hand side.

The idea of the proof: cut $R$ along horizontal segments running left from each zero to the left edge, so that $\log f$ has a single-valued branch on what remains, and integrate $\log f$ around the boundary. Across the cut from a zero $\beta+i\gamma$ the logarithm jumps by $2\pi i$, and the cut has length $\beta-\sigma_0$; the cuts contribute $2\pi\sum(\beta-\sigma_0)$, which equals $2\pi\int_{\sigma_0}^{\sigma_1}\nu(u)\,du$. Comparing imaginary parts gives the formula. We omit the details (see Titchmarsh, Chapter IX).

The useful feature is that the left edge enters only through $\int\log|f|$, and by concavity of the logarithm this is bounded by the logarithm of a mean square. Mean squares of $\zeta$ are exactly what the theory of [[moments]] provides.

blocks.title: A first density bound
blocks.body:
Fix $\tfrac12<\sigma_0<\sigma<1$, with $\sigma_0$ chosen so that no zero of $\zeta$ has real part exactly $\sigma_0$ (this excludes only countably many values). Then as $T\to\infty$
$$N(\sigma,T)\le\Bigl(\frac{\log\zeta(2\sigma_0)}{4\pi(\sigma-\sigma_0)}+o(1)\Bigr)T.$$
In particular $N(\sigma,T)=O_\sigma(T)$ for every fixed $\sigma>\tfrac12$, while $N(T)\sim\frac{T}{2\pi}\log T$.

blocks.title: Proof
blocks.body:
We use two standard facts. First, the mean value theorem: for fixed $\sigma_0>\tfrac12$,
$$\frac1T\int_1^T|\zeta(\sigma_0+it)|^2\,dt\to\zeta(2\sigma_0)\qquad(T\to\infty).$$
Second, $\arg\zeta(u+iT)=O(\log T)$ uniformly for $u\ge\tfrac12$ when $T$ is not the ordinate of a zero (this is the bound behind the error term in the Riemann–von Mangoldt formula). It is enough to treat such $T$: for any $T$, apply the result at a slightly larger admissible $T'$, which only increases $N(\sigma,\cdot)$.

Apply Littlewood's lemma to $f=\zeta$ on the rectangle $\sigma_0\le\mathrm{Re}\,s\le2$, $1\le\mathrm{Im}\,s\le T$. The pole $s=1$ lies outside it; there are no zeros with ordinate in $(0,1]$ (the lowest is near $14.13$), none with real part $\ge1$, and none on the left edge by the choice of $\sigma_0$. So for $\sigma_0\le u\le2$, $\nu(u)$ counts zeros with $\beta>u$ and $0<\gamma\le T$.

Right edge. For $\mathrm{Re}\,s>1$, $\log\zeta(s)=\sum_{n\ge2}\frac{\Lambda(n)}{\log n}n^{-s}$, so
$$\int_1^T\log|\zeta(2+it)|\,dt=\mathrm{Re}\sum_{n\ge2}\frac{\Lambda(n)}{n^2\log n}\int_1^Tn^{-it}\,dt,$$
and $|\int_1^Tn^{-it}dt|\le 2/\log n$. The sum converges, so this term is $O(1)$.

Horizontal edges. The top contributes $O(\log T)$ by the second fact; the bottom is a fixed number.

Left edge. Since $\log$ is concave, Jensen's inequality gives
$$\int_1^T\log|\zeta(\sigma_0+it)|\,dt=\frac12\int_1^T\log|\zeta(\sigma_0+it)|^2\,dt\le\frac{T-1}{2}\log\Bigl(\frac{1}{T-1}\int_1^T|\zeta(\sigma_0+it)|^2dt\Bigr)=\frac T2\bigl(\log\zeta(2\sigma_0)+o(1)\bigr).$$

Putting the pieces together,
$$2\pi\int_{\sigma_0}^{2}\nu(u)\,du\le\frac T2\log\zeta(2\sigma_0)+o(T).$$
Now every zero counted by $N(\sigma,T)$ has $\beta\ge\sigma>u$ for each $u\in[\sigma_0,\sigma)$, so $\nu(u)\ge N(\sigma,T)$ there, and $\nu\ge0$ everywhere. Hence $\int_{\sigma_0}^2\nu\ge(\sigma-\sigma_0)N(\sigma,T)$, and dividing by $2\pi(\sigma-\sigma_0)$ gives $N(\sigma,T)\le\bigl(\frac{\log\zeta(2\sigma_0)}{4\pi(\sigma-\sigma_0)}+o(1)\bigr)T$, which is the theorem.

Taking $\sigma_0$ near $(\sigma+\tfrac12)/2$ gives the clean form $N(\sigma,T)\le\bigl(\frac{\log\zeta(\sigma+1/2)}{2\pi(\sigma-1/2)}+o(1)\bigr)T$. Comparing with $N(T)\sim\frac{T}{2\pi}\log T$: the proportion of zeros with $\beta\ge\sigma$ is $O_\sigma(1/\log T)$.

blocks.title: From O(T) to a power saving: mollifiers and large values
blocks.body:
The argument above is wasteful: $|\zeta|^2$ has mean $\zeta(2\sigma_0)>1$. The stronger theorems first multiply $\zeta$ by a mollifier
$$M_X(s)=\sum_{n\le X}\frac{\mu(n)}{n^{s}},$$
a truncation of $1/\zeta(s)$. Then $\zeta(s)M_X(s)=1+\sum_{n>X}a_nn^{-s}$, where $a_n=\sum_{d\mid n,\ d\le X}\mu(d)$ vanishes for $2\le n\le X$ (Example 4). At a zero $\rho$ the left side is $0$, so the tail $\sum_{n>X}a_n n^{-\rho}$ must equal $-1$: a zero forces a Dirichlet polynomial (after smoothing and shifting the line of integration) to take a large value.

So zero-density becomes a question about large values: given a Dirichlet polynomial $D(t)=\sum_{N<n\le2N}b_nn^{-it}$ and a threshold $V$, how many well-spaced points $t_1,\dots,t_R\in[0,T]$ can have $|D(t_r)|\ge V$? The mean value theorem for Dirichlet polynomials,
$$\int_0^T\Bigl|\sum_{n\le N}b_nn^{-it}\Bigr|^2dt=\sum_{n\le N}(T+O(n))|b_n|^2,$$
due to Montgomery and Vaughan and a relative of the [[large-sieve|large sieve]], gives $R\ll(T+N)\sum|b_n|^2/V^2$ up to logarithms. Ingham's theorem comes essentially from this together with the fourth moment of $\zeta$. Huxley's improvement uses the Halász–Montgomery large values inequality, which does better when $R$ is large. The Guth–Maynard bound comes from a new large values estimate that is strongest near the critical point $\sigma=\tfrac34$ where the older bounds were weakest. In every case the bound is optimised by choosing the mollifier length $X$ and the polynomial lengths as powers of $T$ depending on $\sigma$, which is why the exponents are rational functions of $\sigma$.

blocks.title: Why density is almost as good as RH: primes in short intervals
blocks.body:
The truncated explicit formula ([[explicit-formula]]) says that for $2\le T\le x$
$$\psi(x)=x-\sum_{|\gamma|\le T}\frac{x^{\rho}}{\rho}+O\Bigl(\frac{x}{T}(\log x)^2\Bigr).$$
Subtract the same formula at $x$ from the one at $x+h$. Since $\frac{(x+h)^\rho-x^\rho}{\rho}=\int_x^{x+h}u^{\rho-1}du$ and $|u^{\rho-1}|=u^{\beta-1}\le x^{\beta-1}$,
$$\bigl|\psi(x+h)-\psi(x)-h\bigr|\le h\sum_{|\gamma|\le T}x^{\beta-1}+O\Bigl(\frac{x}{T}(\log x)^2\Bigr).$$
Take $h=x^{\theta}$ and $T=x^{1-\theta+\delta}$ with small $\delta>0$; then the error term is $o(h)$. It remains to show $\sum_{|\gamma|\le T}x^{\beta-1}=o(1)$. Writing $x^{\beta-1}=x^{-1/2}+\int_{1/2}^{\beta}x^{u-1}\log x\,du$ for $\beta\ge\tfrac12$ and using $x^{\beta-1}\le x^{-1/2}$ for $\beta<\tfrac12$,
$$\sum_{|\gamma|\le T}x^{\beta-1}\ll x^{-1/2}\,T\log T+\log x\int_{1/2}^{1}x^{u-1}N(u,T)\,du.$$
The first term is small because $T<x^{1/2-\delta}$ once $\theta>\tfrac12+2\delta$. In the integral, a density bound gives $x^{u-1}N(u,T)\ll(T^A/x)^{1-u}(\log T)^B$. If $T^A\le x^{1-\delta'}$ this is at most $x^{-\delta'(1-u)}(\log T)^B$, and the zero-free region means only $1-u\ge\eta(T)$ matters, where the Vinogradov–Korobov region has $\eta(T)=c(\log T)^{-2/3}(\log\log T)^{-1/3}$. Then $x^{-\delta'\eta(T)}$ decays faster than any power of $\log x$, and the integral is $o(1)$.

The condition $T^A<x^{1-\delta'}$ with $T=x^{1-\theta+\delta}$ means $A(1-\theta)<1$, that is $\theta>1-1/A$.

blocks.title: Density bounds give primes in short intervals
blocks.body:
Suppose $N(\sigma,T)\ll T^{A(1-\sigma)}(\log T)^B$ uniformly for $\tfrac12\le\sigma\le1$. Then for every fixed $\theta>1-\frac1A$,
$$\psi(x+x^{\theta})-\psi(x)\sim x^{\theta}\qquad(x\to\infty),$$
and consequently $p_{n+1}-p_n\ll p_n^{\theta}$.

With Huxley's $A=\tfrac{12}{5}$ this gives $\theta>\tfrac{7}{12}$. Guth and Maynard deduced the corresponding result for every $\theta>\tfrac{17}{30}$. The density hypothesis would give every $\theta>\tfrac12$; RH gives a little more, namely intervals of length $\sqrt x(\log x)^{2+\varepsilon}$, because under RH $\psi(x+h)-\psi(x)=h+O(\sqrt x(\log x)^2)$.

blocks.title: Example 1: bookkeeping with exponents
blocks.body:
(a) Check that Ingham's and Huxley's exponents agree at $\sigma=\tfrac34$, and that the Guth–Maynard exponent agrees with Ingham's at $\sigma=\tfrac7{10}$ and with Huxley's at $\sigma=\tfrac8{10}$.

(b) For $A=3,\ \tfrac{12}{5},\ \tfrac{30}{13},\ 2$, compute the short-interval exponent $1-1/A$.
blocks.solution:
(a) Divide each exponent by $1-\sigma$. Ingham: $3/(2-\sigma)$; Huxley: $3/(3\sigma-1)$; Guth–Maynard: $15/(3+5\sigma)$. At $\sigma=\tfrac34$: $3/(5/4)=\tfrac{12}{5}$ and $3/(5/4)=\tfrac{12}5$. At $\sigma=\tfrac7{10}$: $3/(13/10)=\tfrac{30}{13}$ and $15/(13/2)=\tfrac{30}{13}$. At $\sigma=\tfrac8{10}$: $15/7$ and $3/(7/5)=\tfrac{15}{7}$. Ingham's ratio increases with $\sigma$ and the other two decrease, so on $[\tfrac12,1]$ the best available ratio is largest at the crossing points: $\tfrac{12}5$ at $\tfrac34$ without Guth–Maynard, and $\tfrac{30}{13}$ at $\tfrac7{10}$ with it.

(b) $1-\tfrac13=\tfrac23$; $1-\tfrac5{12}=\tfrac7{12}$; $1-\tfrac{13}{30}=\tfrac{17}{30}$; $1-\tfrac12=\tfrac12$. In decimals: $0.667,\ 0.583,\ 0.567,\ 0.5$.

blocks.title: Example 2: why A cannot be smaller than 2
blocks.body: Show that no bound $N(\sigma,T)\ll T^{A(1-\sigma)}(\log T)^B$ valid uniformly on $\tfrac12\le\sigma\le1$ can have $A<2$, and that $A=2$ forces $B\ge1$.
blocks.solution: Put $\sigma=\tfrac12$. By the symmetry $\rho\mapsto1-\bar\rho$, at least half of the zeros with $0<\gamma\le T$ have $\beta\ge\tfrac12$, so $N(\tfrac12,T)\ge\tfrac12N(T)\ge cT\log T$ for large $T$. The bound would give $cT\log T\ll T^{A/2}(\log T)^B$. If $A<2$, the right side is $o(T)$, a contradiction. If $A=2$, it reads $T\log T\ll T(\log T)^B$, which needs $B\ge1$.

blocks.title: Example 3: when does the first density bound say something?
blocks.body: Take $\sigma=\tfrac34$ in the clean form of the first density bound, ignoring the $o(1)$. Compare $N(\tfrac34,T)\lesssim cT$, with $c=\frac{\log\zeta(5/4)}{2\pi\cdot(1/4)}$, against the trivial bound $N(\tfrac34,T)\le\tfrac12N(T)$, where $N(T)\approx\frac{T}{2\pi}\log\frac{T}{2\pi e}$. Roughly from what height on is the density bound better?
blocks.solution:
We have $\zeta(1.25)\approx4.595$, so $c=\log(4.595)/(\pi/2)\approx1.525/1.571\approx0.971$. The density bound wins when $0.971\,T<\frac{T}{4\pi}\log\frac{T}{2\pi e}$, i.e. $\log\frac{T}{2\pi e}>4\pi\cdot0.971\approx12.2$, i.e. $T$ larger than about $3\times10^6$.

The lesson: a bound $O(T)$ against $N(T)\asymp T\log T$ saves only a logarithm, and logarithms grow slowly. The power-saving theorems save powers of $T$, which is why they, and not this one, are used for primes.

blocks.title: Example 4: the coefficients of ζ times a mollifier
blocks.body:
Let $X\ge1$ and $a_n=\sum_{d\mid n,\ d\le X}\mu(d)$. Show that $a_1=1$, that $a_n=0$ for $2\le n\le X$, and that $|a_n|\le\tau(n)$ for all $n$. Deduce that for $\mathrm{Re}\,s>1$
$$\zeta(s)\sum_{d\le X}\frac{\mu(d)}{d^s}=1+\sum_{n>X}\frac{a_n}{n^s}.$$
blocks.solution:
If $n\le X$, every divisor of $n$ is at most $X$, so $a_n=\sum_{d\mid n}\mu(d)$, which is $1$ for $n=1$ and $0$ for $n>1$ (the basic property of the Möbius function, [[mobius]]). In general $a_n$ is a sum of at most $\tau(n)$ terms each equal to $0$ or $\pm1$, so $|a_n|\le\tau(n)$.

For $\mathrm{Re}\,s>1$ both series converge absolutely, so we may multiply and collect terms with $dm=n$:
$$\zeta(s)\sum_{d\le X}\mu(d)d^{-s}=\sum_{n\ge1}n^{-s}\sum_{d\mid n,\ d\le X}\mu(d)=\sum_n a_nn^{-s},$$
and the terms with $n\le X$ reduce to the single term $1$.

For example with $X=6$: $a_7=\mu(1)=1$, $a_8=\mu(1)+\mu(2)=0$, $a_{12}=\mu(1)+\mu(2)+\mu(3)+\mu(6)=0$, $a_{30}=\mu(1)+\mu(2)+\mu(3)+\mu(5)+\mu(6)=1-1-1-1+1=-1$.

blocks.body:
- A density estimate is not a zero-free region. It allows zeros arbitrarily far to the right of $\tfrac12$ (but not past the zero-free region); it only limits their number. The two kinds of result are used together.
- $T^{A(1-\sigma)}$ is not small near $\sigma=\tfrac12$: there it is at least $T$. Density theorems are informative mainly for $\sigma$ well to the right of $\tfrac12$.
- The placement of $\varepsilon$ matters. $T^{A(1-\sigma)+\varepsilon}$ and $T^{(A+\varepsilon)(1-\sigma)}$ differ exactly near $\sigma=1$, the range that matters most for primes.

Density estimates sit between [[zero-free-region|zero-free regions]], which control $\sigma$ extremely close to $1$, and the full [[rh|Riemann hypothesis]]. Their inputs are mean values of $\zeta$ and of Dirichlet polynomials ([[moments]], [[large-sieve]]); bounds for $\zeta$ on the critical line feed in through Ingham's method, so progress on the [[lindelof|Lindelöf hypothesis]] improves density exponents. The outputs are results on primes in short intervals and gaps between primes ([[prime-patterns]]). For Dirichlet [[l-functions]], density estimates in the modulus aspect, often proved with the large sieve, are a key ingredient of the [[bombieri-vinogradov|Bombieri–Vinogradov theorem]] and of Linnik's theorem on the least prime in an arithmetic progression, where they are combined with the repulsion of [[siegel-zeros|exceptional zeros]].

1. Show that Carlson's exponent $4\sigma(1-\sigma)$ is larger than Ingham's $3(1-\sigma)/(2-\sigma)$ for every $\sigma\in(\tfrac12,1)$, so Carlson's bound is always the weaker one.
2. Deduce from the first density bound that for each fixed $\delta>0$ the proportion of zeros with $0<\gamma\le T$ and $|\beta-\tfrac12|>\delta$ tends to $0$ as $T\to\infty$.
3. In the proof of the first density bound, replace the mean value theorem by the pointwise bound $|\zeta(\sigma_0+it)|\ll|t|^{1/2}$. What bound for $N(\sigma,T)$ do you get, and why is it useless?
4. Following the short-interval argument, find the exponent $\theta$ that a hypothetical bound $N(\sigma,T)\ll T^{\frac{5}{2}(1-\sigma)}(\log T)^{10}$ would give.

sources.ref: E. C. Titchmarsh, The Theory of the Riemann Zeta-Function, 2nd ed. revised by D. R. Heath-Brown
H. Iwaniec and E. Kowalski, Analytic Number Theory
